# The Data

```{r}
#| label: data
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# install packages: install.packages("package")
# load packages
library(tidyverse) 
library(knitr)
library(gtsummary)
library(ggstatsplot)
library(downlit)
library(broom)
library(here)

# load data
df <- read_csv(here("Data", "my_dataset.csv"))

df <- df |>
  mutate(
    `stress` = factor(
     `Financial Stress Rating`, 
      levels = c("[ 1 ] Low Stress (Rarely worry about money for school)", "[ 2 ] Moderate Stress (Sometimes worry about managing expenses)", "[ 3 ] High Stress (Constantly worry or struggle with school expenses)"), 
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  ) |>
  select(
    stress = `Financial Stress Rating`,
    daily = `Daily Allowance`,
  )
```

## Financial Stress and Daily Allowance Dataset

The data was collected from a student survey examining daily spending budgets and self-reported financial stress levels.

A data frame with 68 observations on 2 numerical variables.

- `stress` Low Stress, Moderate Stress, High Stress.

- `daily` Daily Allowance in PHP

The first 6 rows of the data set are shown in @tbl-survey

```{r}
#| label: tbl-survey
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| error: false
#| tbl-cap: "The first 6 observations of the data set."

df |> 
  head() |> # get the first six rows of the data
  kable(col.names = c("Financial Stress Rating", "Daily Allowance")) # create a table
```

## Descriptive Statistics

The mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum of `stress`(Financial Stress Rating) and `daily`(Daily Allowance) in the data set are shown in @tbl-summary. There is a total of 68 observations.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Summary statistics of `daily` when grouped according to `stress`."
#| message: false

df |> # call the data
  tbl_summary( # create a table
    by = stress, # group by Financial Stress Rating
    include = daily, # select numerical variable
    label = list(daily ~ "Daily Allowance"), # clean row label
    statistic = all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ± {sd} ({min} - {max})", # descriptive statistics
    digits = all_continuous() ~ 2 # no. of digits (rounding)
  )
```

# Hypothesis Testing

## Research Question

Is there a significant difference in daily allowance across the three financial stress rating levels (Low Stress, Moderate Stress, and High Stress)?

## Hypothesis and Test Statistics

- $H_0$: The distribution (median) of daily allowance is the same across all three financial stress rating levels.

- $H_a$: At least one financial stress rating level has a different daily allowance distribution (median).

- **Test Statistic:** Kruskal-Wallis $H$ test (or $\chi^2$ approximation) at $\alpha = 0.05$.

- **Kruskal-Wallis test** (non-parametric test comparing medians across 3 independent groups)

- Independent observations across the three financial stress rating groups ($n = 68$).

## Results and Interpretation

The box plot and test statistics are shown in @fig-test.

```{r}
#| label: fig-test
#| fig-cap: Box plot of daily allowance across financial stress ratings with Kruskal-Wallis test results.

#| fig-height: 5
#| warning: false
#| error: false
#| message: false

ggbetweenstats(
  data = df,
  x = stress,
  y = daily,
  type = "nonparametric", 
  xlab = "Financial Stress Rating",
  ylab = "Daily Allowance"
) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Low Stress", "Moderate Stress", "High Stress")) +
  labs(caption = NULL)
```

Based on the box plot and the *p*-value being less than 5% (*p*-value = $8.89 \times 10^{-4}$, $\chi^2_{\text{Kruskal-Wallis}}(2) = 14.05$), we reject the null hypothesis. There is strong evidence of a significant difference in daily allowance across the three financial stress rating levels ($\hat{\varepsilon}^2_{\text{ordinal}} = 0.21$, indicating a moderate-to-large effect size). Specifically, median daily allowance decreases as financial stress increases, dropping from 225.00 in the Low Stress group ($n = 10$) to 150.00 in the Moderate Stress group ($n = 42$) and 100.00 in the High Stress group ($n = 16$).
